title: Media Queries
summary: Detailed look at @media rules: max-width, min-width, combining both with and, plus the screen/print media types. The exercise builds four breakpoints that change the body background colour for mobile, tablet, laptop and desktop widths.

concepts.heading: Anatomy of a media query
points: Written in place of a selector: @media (condition) { normal rules }. The rules inside only apply when the condition is true, and they override the default styles outside the block.
@media (max-width: 600px) means 'viewport at most 600px wide'. Typical use: shrink an h1, or reduce a 200x200 blue div to 100x100 on phones.
@media (min-width: 600px) flips direction: it targets viewports 600px and wider, i.e. the bigger-screen end.
Think of the width axis from 0 to roughly 2400px: max-width styles the left portion up to the breakpoint, min-width styles everything to the right.

concepts.heading: Combining conditions
points: Join conditions with the keyword and: @media (min-width: 600px) and (max-width: 900px) targets only widths in that band.

The same pattern can express 'outside a band' by reversing which side each limit is on (small max-width plus separate larger min-width rule). Read each limit literally: max-width is the highest width where the rules apply, min-width the lowest.
(Extra) Boundaries are inclusive, so adjacent bands should differ by 1px (480 / 481) to avoid overlap.

concepts.heading: Media types and other features
points: You may see screen, as in @media screen and (max-width: 600px). Screen is effectively the default so it is rarely needed; the other common type is print, which applies rules only when the page is printed.
MDN's 'Using media queries' page lists more features: orientation, height, width, device-width and device-height, and media types. Most real work only needs min-width and max-width.

concepts.heading: Testing in Chrome DevTools
points: Open DevTools (Chrome menu, More tools, Developer tools) and toggle the device toolbar.
Choose a preset (iPhone SE, iPhone 12, iPad Air) or Responsive and drag or type an exact width to check which breakpoint triggers.

code_examples.caption: max-width, min-width and both

task.name: Device-width background colours
task.starting_point: index.html with body background aquamarine and TODO comments listing four ranges: Mobile 319-480px, tablets 481-1200px, laptops 1201-1600px, desktops 1601px and up. An empty body.
task.goal: Make the body background change by width, matching solution.html: lightsalmon (mobile), powderblue (tablet), limegreen (laptop), seagreen (desktop).
steps: Add @media (min-width: 319px) and (max-width: 480px) with body { background-color: lightsalmon } (max-width alone also works since few screens are narrower than 320px).
Add @media (min-width: 1601px) with seagreen; no max needed.
Test by resizing the browser or the DevTools device toolbar.
task.expected_result: Resizing the window flips the page between four colours at 480/481, 1200/1201 and 1600/1601px; wider than 1601 is seagreen. Below 319px the default aquamarine shows.

pitfalls: Mixing up max and min direction (max-width styles smaller screens).
Overlapping or gapping ranges, such as 480 to 482.
Forgetting the viewport meta tag, so phones report a wide viewport.
Omitting the parentheses around each condition.

playground.coverage: Tasks cover the tablet and laptop bands only; the explore simulator shows min-width breakpoints with a live preview; notes cover anatomy, conditions, mobile-first and common breakpoints.
gaps_and_ideas: Add the missing mobile (lightsalmon, 319-480) and desktop (seagreen, 1601+) tasks so all four colours from the course exercise are practised.
Add an explicit max-width vs min-width diagram of the width axis.
Add a 'print' media query task with the browser's print preview.
Mention Chrome DevTools device toolbar for testing, in case the playground preview width selector is unavailable in real projects.
